🇸🇴 Somalia ready to provide Ethiopia with port access, won’t accept Israeli presence in Somaliland
 
Mogadishu is ready to provide its landlocked neighbor with access to two or three of its ports for commercial imports and exports, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has told Al-Jazeera.
The port access would presumably be contingent on Ethiopia annulling its 2024 port access MoU with the Somali breakaway of Somaliland, which has yet to be fully implemented amid negotiations with Somalia.
📹 In the interview, Hassan Sheikh also commented on Israeli attempts [to set up a presence in Somaliland](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74720), emphasizing that Mogadishu would not tolerate such a presence “under any circumstances.”
At the same time, the Somali president accused the Houthis – Israel’s key regional adversaries, of being [“aggressive” and of “destabilizing”](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74031) Yemen and the region.
👉 This can be explained by Somalia’s signing of a major military cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia in February and its longstanding alliance with Turkey, another member of the new Mecca defense pact.
Hassan Sheikh’s government currently controls as little as 20% of Somalia’s sovereign territory, including just one major port – Mogadishu. Al-Qaeda ally Al-Shabaab controls of ~30% of the country, Somaliland about 22%, and semi-autonomous states like Puntland and Jubaland much of the rest (including the major ports of Bosaso and Kismayo).

Spontaneous demonstrations, song and dance broke out in the critical Taiz governorate town of At Turbah on Sunday as Houthi fighters in pickups entered it.
📍Local residents were seen greeting and mingling with fighters, who chanted their famed Sarkha slogan as they rode through town.
At Turbah sits directly at the intersection of a critical highway link connecting the city of Taiz to Aden, capital of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. events.text:
🇺🇸☢️ US attempt to put nuclear reactor on the Moon before China and Russia could end in disaster
 
“There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn,” Union of Concerned Scientists nuclear safety director Edwin Lyman told NYT.
From space rockets exploding on the launch pad or overhead, to meteorite strikes and a harsh lunar climate (no atmosphere, no water, severe temperature swings and highly abrasive, electrostatically charged Moon dust), an accident involving even a small reactor threatens to produce much more radioactive fallout than on Earth, and turn entire swathes of the Moon into an exclusion zone.
🛰 Then there’s the matter of experience. NYT surprisingly admitted that “no country has more experience than Russia” when it comes to space-based reactor technology, citing 30+ deployments aboard Soviet-era satellites. Russia also “controls the largest supply of what is considered the safest nuclear fuel for space missions”: HALEU – a low-enriched fuel the US doesn’t have the ability to produce at scale.
The US also hasn’t built a space-grade reactor since the 1960s, and despite spending $20B+ in this area since then, has yet to field a new, working design with adequate heat dissipation, shielding and structural integrity characteristics.
That makes US plans to put a reactor on the Moon as soon as 2030 – a full six years before China and Russia hope to do so, fraught with risk.

🔥 Houthis put Aden-based government’s second-most-important stronghold into a giant cauldron
 
The situation in Taiz governorate, a key strategic crossroads, industrial hub, agricultural center and physical buffer between the Ansar Allah-aligned northern Yemeni government and its Saudi-backed southern adversary, is growing desperate.
Simultaneous Houthi offensives southwest and southeast of Taiz City have reportedly won them control over virtually all key roads into and out of the city, including sections of the main highway between Taiz City and Aden.
📹 Houthi-affiliated media reported Sunday that the Yemeni Armed Forces had entered Al-Turbah, a mountainous highland town directly overlooking the highway, and that enemy forces had been expelled from the town, as well as the broader Al-Shamayatayn and Sami districts of Taiz governorate.
The Saudi-backed government reported the targeting of “hundreds” of Houthi positions on the Taiz front in the past 24 hours, but that apparently proved insufficient to stop their advance. Pro-Ansar Allah social media have posted a video of what they say is Saudi warplanes bombing their own allies after they fled the battlefield.

🇮🇶🛢 Iraq sends 2M barrels beyond Hormuz in export shift
Iraq’s state tanker company has arranged a VLCC carrying 2M barrels of crude to sail beyond the Strait of Hormuz, marking its first such move in decades.
By taking responsibility for moving the cargo outside the Persian Gulf, Baghdad is trying to make Iraqi crude easier to buy for refiners wary of Hormuz disruptions and reduce the discounts needed to move barrels from Basra.
Iraq is also seeking funds to expand its own tanker fleet while pursuing alternative export routes through Turkey and potentially Syria.

📍🪖 Yemen's Saudi-backed government launches operation to retake Houthi-held territory
Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, has announced military operations to retake remaining Houthi-held territory and restore state authority across the country, Al Jazeera reports.
💬 "We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis," he said.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition backing the government, which the Houthis had driven out of Sanaa. Fighting has intensified since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July. 
Despite the counteroffensive, the Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground:
🟥 they seized the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in a [lightning offensive](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75488) that saw government forces collapse
🟥 they've made gains on strategic hilltops near [Taiz](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75564) — advancing on the last road between the city and Aden, where the Saudi-backed government is based
Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit of the Red Sea — a key shipping route that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the effectively closed Strait of Hormuz.

events.text:
🤔🤥 Why is Trump holding back from bombing the Houthis?
 
President Donald Trump has so far avoided reopening direct US strikes on Yemen’s Houthis, despite renewed pressure on Saudi Arabia and growing concerns over Red Sea shipping, Politico reported.
The main constraints are practical:
 
🔴 Operation Rough Rider, last year's US air campaign against the Houthis, delivered limited results — even as Trump declared the Houthis had "capitulated"
🔴 The Iran war has strained US munitions stocks, making another sustained campaign harder to justify
🔴 The Houthis are currently pledging not to attack American ships, reducing the immediate pressure on Washington to intervene
Former US envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said Washington has little incentive to open another front while the conflict with Iran remains unresolved. 
🔍The Houthis have meanwhile become a far more capable force, expanding local weapons production, modifying Iranian-supplied missiles, and reportedly integrating AI into parts of their arsenal. Western officials cited in the report said that even reduced Iranian support would not necessarily cripple the group.
The emerging calculation in Washington is that containing the Houthis may be cheaper than trying to defeat them outright, especially while the US is already managing simultaneous crises in Iran, Gaza, and Ukraine.
